domains.name: Humanities, history and philosophy of inquiry
Emerging and prospective research spaces
branches: computational epistemology (formal models of how claims gain or lose warrant)
cross-scale causal science (methods linking molecular, organismal, ecological and social scales)
machine-assisted experimental design as a distinct methodology
multi-modal mathematics (formal relations among symbolic, geometric, visual and embodied representations)
reproducibility engineering (science of executable provenance and independent replication)
planetary systems observability (integrated Earth, infrastructure and ecological measurement)
synthetic cognitive ecology (interactions among human, machine and institutional cognition)
xenomathematics (user-proposed exploratory program; definitions and theorems required)
glyph and n-ality mathematics (exploratory representation-theoretic program; formal objects required)
temporal structure science (cross-disciplinary study of time, periodicity, memory and phase)
quantum-enabled metrology and information science (bounded by demonstrated physical effects)

historical_programs.label: Alchemy
historical_programs.lesson: Preserved experimental practices and material knowledge while its theoretical framework was transformed by modern chemistry.

historical_programs.label: Phlogiston theory
historical_programs.lesson: A useful case for studying how measurement, mass balance and new explanatory frameworks displaced a dominant theory.

historical_programs.label: Caloric theory
historical_programs.lesson: Shows how heat moved from a material-fluid picture toward energy and statistical mechanics.

historical_programs.label: Vitalism
historical_programs.lesson: Useful for tracing disputes about mechanism, emergence and biological explanation; not a current substitute for biochemical accounts.

historical_programs.label: Luminiferous ether
historical_programs.lesson: Shows how a background medium was motivated, tested and abandoned as relativity and experiment changed the problem.

historical_programs.label: Phrenology
historical_programs.lesson: A cautionary example of weak measurement, confirmation bias and social prejudice dressed as scientific certainty.

historical_programs.label: Humoral medicine
historical_programs.lesson: Study as a historical explanatory system, not as a modern clinical guide.

historical_programs.label: Miasma theory
historical_programs.lesson: Contrasts environmental observation with later microbial causal evidence.

reading_list.title: Newton's Principia: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy
reading_list.creator: Isaac Newton; English translation by Andrew Motte
reading_list.rights: Public domain; Library of Congress rights statement
reading_list.context: A synthesis of mathematical mechanics and celestial motion, shaped by the astronomical work of Copernicus, Kepler and observational data available in the seventeenth century. Read the definitions, laws, scholia and geometric demonstrations as a historical mathematical practice, not as a modern textbook.
questions: What does Newton define before proving anything?
How are mathematical laws connected to observations of planetary motion?
Which assumptions are explicit, and which belong to the period's natural philosophy?
How did later mechanics reinterpret the work?

reading_list.title: On the Origin of Species
reading_list.creator: Charles Darwin
reading_list.rights: Public domain; Smithsonian Libraries CC0 record
reading_list.context: Read the first edition in Darwin's own publication context: he records Beagle observations, years of accumulating evidence, the independent work of Alfred Russel Wallace, collaboration with Lyell and Hooker, and the limits of his compressed abstract. Compare the sixth edition's later historical sketch to see how priority and predecessor histories were revised.
questions: How did Darwin combine biogeography, geology, domestication, classification and embryology?
Why did he publish an abstract before the full evidence was complete?
How did he state difficulties and alternative evidence?
What did he acknowledge about Wallace, Hooker and Lyell?
How did the 1872 historical sketch revise the story of prior ideas?

reading_list.title: Traité élémentaire de chimie
reading_list.creator: Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier; with major visual and editorial contributions by Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier
reading_list.rights: Public Domain Mark / CC0 item records
reading_list.context: Lavoisier's chemical program emphasized quantitative measurement, the balance, systematic nomenclature and a reorganization of combustion and matter. Paulze Lavoisier contributed illustrations and helped transmit chemical knowledge. Study the instruments, tables, terminology and experimental procedures alongside the argument.
questions: Why does mass measurement matter to the argument?
How are experiments described so others can repeat them?
How does a new nomenclature change what can be reasoned about?
Who contributed to the work beyond the named author?

reading_list.title: Novum Organum
reading_list.creator: Francis Bacon; English edition edited by Joseph Devey
reading_list.context: Bacon argues for disciplined inquiry aided by intellectual instruments, gradual induction from particulars, and awareness of systematic sources of error. The text read is a 1902 English edition, not Bacon's original-language text.
questions: How does Bacon distinguish dogmatism from disciplined uncertainty?
What are the four idols and how do they distort inquiry?
Why does he compare intellectual aids to mechanical instruments?
Which parts of his method survive in modern research, and which need revision?

reading_list.title: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding
reading_list.creator: David Hume; edited by L. A. Selby-Bigge
reading_list.context: Hume studies how impressions, ideas, custom and repeated experience shape belief. His analysis of causal inference and induction is a foundation for asking what scientific evidence can justify. The digital text is a later edited edition.
questions: How do ideas relate to impressions?
Why does custom shape expectations about cause and effect?
Why doesn't repeated past experience deductively prove future regularity?
What does this imply for model validation and prediction?

reading_list.title: The Elements of Geometrie
reading_list.creator: Euclid; translated by Henry Billingsley, with contributions by John Dee and others
reading_list.domain: mathematics / geometry / history of mathematical transmission
reading_list.context: A CC0 digitized 1570 English edition that shows how Euclid's geometry was transmitted and taught in early modern England. It is a historical translation and reception artifact, not the ancient Greek original.
questions: How are definitions, postulates and propositions organized?
How did the 1570 translation and its paratext shape the reception of Greek geometry?
What role did commentary, diagrams and printing play in mathematical education?
How does an axiomatic proof structure differ from experimental evidence?

cross_domain_relationships.label: geochemistry
cross_domain_relationships.scope_rationale: Earth materials and processes are the primary object; chemical methods and theory are integral secondary methods.

cross_domain_relationships.label: chemical engineering
cross_domain_relationships.scope_rationale: The discipline's primary focus is design and operation of processes and systems, with chemistry as its core scientific foundation.

cross_domain_relationships.label: physiology
cross_domain_relationships.scope_rationale: The field studies functions of living systems; medical physiology is an applied health-science context.

cross_domain_relationships.label: systems biology
cross_domain_relationships.relationship: Cross-scale systems analysis of living systems
cross_domain_relationships.scope_rationale: It is explicitly interdisciplinary, integrating biological objects with mathematical, computational and systems methods.

cross_domain_relationships.label: neuroscience
cross_domain_relationships.relationship: Nervous systems, cognition and clinical translation
cross_domain_relationships.scope_rationale: The primary home is the study of nervous systems and behavior; clinical neuroscience is a secondary medical context.
